claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and exhibits brittle fracture.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries cause local stress concentrations and brittle fracture in the untreated alloy.
Rapid thermal annealing can trigger localized precipitation at the lamellar interfaces.
Rapid thermal annealing produces nanoscale precipitates preferentially along lamellar colony boundaries.
The boundary precipitates absorb and re-emit dislocations.
Absorption and re-emission of dislocations by the precipitates redistributes stress and reduces local stress concentrations.
Reduced local stress concentrations suppress microcracking and delay crack nucleation.
The precipitates promote more homogeneous plastic flow.
The precipitates pin dislocations and thereby maintain or enhance yield strength.
Rapid thermal annealing is predicted to increase room-temperature tensile elongation by approximately 50% relative to the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy is predicted to have yield strength equal to or slightly higher than the untreated alloy.
The predicted benefits apply to room-temperature tensile testing at conventional strain rates under ambient conditions.
The benefits may diminish at high temperatures or high strain rates because different deformation mechanisms may prevail.
Annealing temperature and duration must be optimized to obtain the desired precipitate distribution without coarsening or undesirable phase transformations.
The scalability and reproducibility of the treatment on industrially relevant sample sizes remain unverified.
